designs.name: Hold cap: while P4d holds, the mark may not move further from E than where it stood
designs.summary: OWN_HOLD_CAP=1. While the band holds, its edge on the side away from E is the centre the hold began from (R0), so a hold can stop the mark following E but not push it further away. Tested in three versions.
designs.plain: While the mark refuses to follow a disputed feed, it also refuses to move further away from it.

robust.note: Against the book prop it works (+6% wall at $1-5M per block: mark lift 621 to 115 bp, vault value loss $69-111k to $23k). But each version breaks another protection. R0 = stepped centre: a 5-min -5% print is followed after one 150 s step (-507 bp). R0 = centre at the hold's start: a hold confirmed one update late starts from the bad print (AMZN 30 s -5%: -475 bp), and a stuck feed can no longer follow xyz's real crash (value vs E -$283k instead of +$8k). R0 = last agreeing centre, capped only while E is live: prints and stuck feed restored, but E often does not change between two 3 s updates in a crash, the cap drops out and the wall gets through again (621 bp).

losses.note: Crash and quiet-day results identical to the package (the hold never fires there).

traders.note: No effect outside holds.

tests.title: Price discovery: when does xyz lead the feed?
tests.spec: Illiquid coins and price discovery screen (2026-11-05)

tests.setup: Episodes where |P − E| > 1% for 2+ minutes, outside US regular hours; resolved over the next 30 min: feed moved half way toward xyz ('xyz led'), xyz came back ('reverted'), else unresolved. Regime = the relayer's own (oracle = E: external; oracle ≠ E: internal), by majority of the episode's minutes.

tests.title: Book prop beyond the band (P4b) during the GOOGL crash
tests.question: Can an attacker who also holds the xyz book beyond the band freeze P4b's band, and at what cost?
tests.setup: ATTACK_PROP: a fresh account keeps a buy limit at P0 = mid × 1.06 (347.36) from C − 5 s, re-placed every block ($0.2M, $1M, $5M per block, 60 s). It lifts every ask ≤ P0; post-only maker asks below P0 sell to it instead of being pruned. Lower bound on cost from the real tape: every real taker sell in the window fills at P0, valued at E at the end.
findings: In the replay the attacker could not hold the book. At $0.2–5M per block it bought 359–421k shares ($112–132M) in 60 s, but its bid was never standing at a relayer update and P4b's band never held. The replayed makers are open loop and keep re-quoting near the feed, so this volume is an artefact, not a cost estimate.

Lower bound from the real tape (taker sells only, makers ignored): the attacker buys $20.2M of selling in the first minute (23.5k of the 65k shares forced) and loses at least $2.8M; $5.0M over 5 min; $7.5M over 15 min.

If it succeeds (analytic, not replayed): with the book and P both at P0, P4b's mark goes to R0(1 + d) = 343.9, i.e. +13% above the crashed feed. Today's formula and P2 cap the same attacker at E(1 + d) ≈ 320 (+5%). P4b's extra exposure is the genuine move while the band holds.
Every arbitrageur would sell into a bid 13% above the stock, so the real cost is far above the lower bound.

tests.title: Vault unwind: how fast, and at what price
tests.question: Once the vault has inherited, which unwind loses least without betting on where the price goes next?
tests.setup: Real vault fills decomposed exactly against the external price E (sim/unwind_decomp.py): cushion at takeover, drift (inventory × E's moves), execution (fills vs E). Then the engine's unwind on the replayed book (sim/vault_runs.sh, sim/vault_decomp.py), for today's rules and for P4d + restore-to-IM. Policies: clip (today: 0.5% of inventory per update, a taker IOC), c2 / c5 (2% / 5%), fair (the clip plus every bid at or above E), fair0 (only those bids). Drift is exact for a given schedule (E is the underlying's price, exogenous to xyz); execution relies on a book whose makers do not react, so no vault PnL is reported.
findings: Real vault, decomposed: GOOGL cushion −$48k, drift −$135k, execution +$0.8k; INTC −$68k / −$34k / +$0.6k; AMZN −$48k / +$0.5k / +$0.3k. The sum matches the realized PnL within $1.5k. The sales themselves cost nothing against E (+1 to +2.6 bp); the losses are the takeover price and the price moving while the vault holds.
Faster clips cut exposure but sell below E: 5% per update cuts inventory exposure from $107M·min to $10M·min (today's rules), at −$22k execution vs E (−9 to −27 bp).

The fair sweep sells as fast as the book pays fair value: exposure $107M → $24M·min (today's rules) and $118M → $10M·min (P4d + restore), drift risk (1 sd) $47k → $26k and $59k → $14k, and execution vs E improves (+$6k / +$14k). Sold below E: $3.4M → $1.2M (the clip part only).
On GOOGL the book held $4.8M of bids above E after the takeovers (today's rules): the xyz book lags the feed in a gap, so the stale bids are the cheapest exit.

Realized drift is path luck: GOOGL and INTC kept falling (faster unwinds lost less), AMZN rebounded (they lost more). The fair sweep is chosen for expectation and risk, not for these paths: a sale at or above fair value beats holding in expectation whichever way the price goes.
Selling only to those bids (fair0) stalls when the book trades below fair (xyz leading the feed); keeping the clip guarantees progress.
Needs a HyperCore change (the backstop's unwind orders are protocol-generated). No new constant: the limit is the oracle price.

Normal days: 640 hand-overs, the hold never fires (test handover-screen). The cost of the rule: a real hand-over gap > 10% that xyz has not priced during the internal session is followed at one band width per 150 s instead of at once.

tests.title: The full package, layer by layer, on every event
tests.question: Do P4d, restore-to-IM and the fair sweep work together, and does any layer undo another?

tests.title: Vault capital as a function of all xyz positions: stress curve, worst case, probabilities
tests.question: Given every xyz position today, how much capital does the vault need in a worst case, and how likely is each level?
tests.setup: sim/capital_risk.py: C(positions, r) = the gap model of joint-capital (instant move, positions below 2/3 MM taken over, C = MM of inherited inventory - inherited equity). Stress: every market by the same x. History: today's positions under every real hour and 4 hours. Probabilities: one peak per day, generalized Pareto above the 85th percentile, 500 bootstrap refits for 90% intervals; backtest fit on the first 60% of days. Worst cases: the worst real hour, the broadest selloff hour and the worst 4 hours scaled 1-3x. A Student-t factor model was tried first and rejected (tails fit with < 2 degrees of freedom; 22 hours predicted above $0.93M, none real).
findings: Stress curve on today's positions: every market -3% needs $0.66M, -5% $2.6M, -7.5% $6.0M, -10% $10.6M, -20% $46M (up moves are similar: +5% $1.45M, +10% $10.5M).
Probabilities (today's positions, history's hourly moves): the vault's $1.84M is exceeded in about 10% of years (90% interval 0-49%); $3M in 1.5% (0-24%); $5M in 0.2% (0-10%).
Need exceeded once in Y years: 1 y $0.95M (0.59-1.49), 10 y $1.85M (0.83-5.1), 100 y $3.3M (0.96-18). 209 days of history: 10-100-year levels are extrapolations, hence the wide intervals.
Backtest (fit on 125 days, tested on 84): days above $0.2M predicted 8.2 / observed 5, $0.3M 3.8 / 3, $0.5M 0.8 / 3 (the late-October crash cluster); the tail is if anything under-predicted.
Worst cases: worst real 4 hours $3.0M; the 10-28 hour doubled $5.1M; the 11-05 selloff hour tripled $8.3M; the worst 4 hours doubled $14.9M; every market at its worst at once $2.4M.
Not included: mark-path events such as SKHX 07-27 (single market, $2.6M today, $1.03M under the lead). The instant gap overstates stock gaps (0.25-2.4x measured).

tests.title: Which isolated-only markets are eligible for cross margin
tests.question: Under Hyperliquid's HIP-3 rules (liquidity, reliable oracle, manipulation resilience; no 50% daily moves more than once a month), which of the 98 isolated-only markets could trade.xyz move to cross margin?
tests.setup: sim/cross_eligibility.py. Bars from precedent, the weakest of the 22 cross-enabled markets: listed underlying (spec index; a live pre-IPO fails), 50%-move days < 1 per month, largest daily move <= SNDK's 35.2%, median daily xyz volume >= AMZN's $8.03M, at least a month of candles. ADL and capital from nocross-rank. Sources: HIP-3 spec (cross margin is irreversible, validator-enforced eligibility, 50% move -> slashing review), trade.xyz docs (backstop liquidator only for cross-enabled assets).
findings: 6 of 98 eligible: HOOD, MSTR, NBIS, AMD, EWY, SMSN; $167M of OI (a quarter of the isolated-only total).
Failures: liquidity 87, largest daily move 14 (UNITREE, CXMT, SOXL, KIOXIA, MRVL, ...), history 5, oracle 2; none has had a 50% day more than once a month.

Crossing the six cuts the isolated-only ADL of the worst real hour from $10.0M to $6.8M and of the worst 4 hours from $28.0M to $17.4M (gap model); the vault's 4-hour worst rises from $3.0M to $3.6M (all 98 crossed: $5.6M).

journal.body: Scenario vault PnL depends on an unwind we cannot simulate, so it is never a result. Designs are scored on inherited notional and value at takeover (fair = Binance or E), with ADL shortfall and trader cost as constraints.

journal.title: Margin rules: concentration works, per-account rules split
journal.body: Tiers cut GOOGL's inherited notional sharply, but splitting across accounts escapes any per-account rule. The cluster rule is split-proof but needs Hyperliquid.

journal.title: The lag is the 50 bp clamp
journal.body: Today's takeovers start underwater because the mark lags the stock by 1–3 minutes. Removing the clamp fixes value at takeover; a faster mark also hands the GOOGL whale to the vault whole.

journal.title: Rejected: Binance in the mark; book impact mid
journal.body: Competitor feeds are never inputs. Impact mid relies on the book and a fixed $100k. Retained: P2 (ET), median of E, recent voluntary xyz trades, and the book, with a self-calibrated window.

journal.title: Free put is not profitable with full costs
journal.body: The earlier +$52.7k was gross. With buy-back slippage and fees it loses in every variant; the value transfer past bankruptcy is what remains, and an on-time mark removes it.

journal.title: Why the clamp exists: bad prints
journal.body: The clamp only stops a one-update spike. A 30 s −5% print walks today's mark −4.1%; without the clamp it also sends $2.21M of healthy positions to the vault. P2 ignores it (25–43 bp). The residual is the discovery bound anchored on the spiked E: P3.

journal.title: Criteria fixed by the user
journal.body: In order: robust to attacks; ADL and vault losses; few Hyperliquid changes; traders don't feel it; simple to explain. Validate on the three crashes and on normal markets; a real price-discovery event in a second round.

journal.title: Where I stood (before the P3 test)
journal.body: Against the criteria, P2 is the lead: deployer-only, robust on every test so far, same crash scores as removing the clamp, explainable as 'middle of three prices'. Two things keep it from a recommendation: no normal-market comparison with today (criterion 4), and the bound leak (P3, untested). P1 is simpler but fails robustness. Margin rules only matter for inherited notional; the cluster rule is the only split-proof one and needs Hyperliquid, so it is a second ask. AMZN's 5.6% in two updates beats every mark: nothing in the mark can fix it. Next: normal-market validation of P2 vs today, then the P3 spike test.

journal.title: P3 tested: the band itself is the hole
journal.body: A median anchor over 10 updates stops only prints shorter than 15 s; over 20 updates it stops −5% prints up to 30 s at no measurable crash cost. The bigger finding came from a −20% print: today's formula, P1 and P2 all walk the mark −9.6% in 30 s and send $5.3M of healthy GOOGL positions to the vault, because the band is centred on the bad price and the band always wins. My earlier 'P2 ignores bad prints' only held for prints smaller than the band. P2 is no worse than today here, but no better either. Next: decide how the band should be anchored. Longer windows trade print-length protection against lag in real gaps; I want to test N = 40 and 60 before inventing something new. Engine note: HyperCore's 1% cap had to be switched on for today's formula, where it now binds.

journal.title: Band design: what the band is for decides how to anchor it
journal.body: The band has two opposite jobs. Against an xyz push (book and trades moved, feed right) it must hold the mark near the feed. Against a bad feed (feed wrong, xyz right) it must not follow the feed. From one snapshot the two cases look the same: feed and xyz disagree. What separates them is who agrees with whom over time and what each costs: real xyz trades cost money; a feed error costs the attacker nothing. Options: (1) longer median window, simple but protects only prints shorter than half the window and adds lag in real gaps; (2) P4, the band follows the feed only while xyz trades agree within the band, else it holds; no lag when the market moves together, which is what all three crashes showed; (3) centring on median(feed, trades, previous mark) fails the xyz-push case, since the previous mark drifts with the push; rejected on paper; (4) dropping the band from the trade input breaks trade.xyz's published rule and removes the push defence. My pick to test: P4, with P3 N = 20 as the fallback.

journal.title: P4 works: the band should follow agreement, not the feed
journal.body: Rule: the band follows the stock's price only while xyz trades agree with it within the band. Results: identical to P2 in the three crashes (the band never held, even on AMZN's 5.6% in two updates); every bad print I tried, −5% or −20%, 3 s to 5 min, moved the mark at most 29 bp with no liquidations, where today and P2 lose up to 16% and send $7M of healthy positions to the vault; a stuck feed at crash onset is as good as P2 and far better than today. It adds one sentence and no parameter. P4 replaces P2 as my lead. Open: normal-market comparison with today (still the top gap for criterion 4), illiquid coins where P can go stale, and a feed-plus-trades attacker.

journal.title: Normal markets: traders would not notice P4
journal.body: Ran P4 in every out-of-hours session of the three tapes (≈17 h per coin), regular hours unchanged. Its mark is a median 0.6–0.9 bp from today's, stays as close to the stock, and is no jumpier. About the same accounts are liquidated (252 vs 261). Stop counts looked alarming until I checked sizes: the extra stops are dust orders sitting at the mark (0.7 shares in total on GOOGL). Funding does not change, since today's oracle already equals the feed outside gaps. Turning P4 on all day leaves the crash results unchanged. So on these three days P4 meets every criterion I can measure: robust to every bad-feed case tried, same crash scores as removing the clamp, deployer-only, invisible in normal markets, one sentence to explain. What it does not fix: AMZN-style gaps above 1% per update and the whale reaching the vault whole (margin side). Before I would call it a recommendation: quiet days, an illiquid coin, and the round-2 price-discovery event.

journal.title: Margin: a scheduled leverage cut beats every per-account rule
journal.body: With P4 the mark is on time, so the vault's problem was size: $12.76M inherited. Halving max leverage from 30 minutes before the earnings close to an hour after takes that to $0.02M with takeovers at break-even, on all three coins including AMZN's too-fast gap, and splitting the whale changes nothing because the rule applies to everyone. It is deployer-only and one sentence. The cluster rule, my previous Hyperliquid ask, now does worse ($1.51M, AMZN untouched), so I would not ask Hyperliquid for it. The cost is real: $17.3M of margin for 1.5 h and more shares force-closed (fewer accounts, larger ones, partly market makers the replay cannot adapt), and it rests on traders topping up. Fixed a model bug on the way: accounts taken over were reopened by the replay with zero margin and taken over hundreds of times (only visible at 5x). Current best package: P4 + half leverage around earnings, both deployer-only.

journal.title: Rejected: leverage cuts around earnings
journal.body: The user's point: earnings is where traders want to express an opinion, and lowering max leverage right then would read as the venue stepping in against them. That is criterion 4 (traders don't feel it) seen from the product side, which my scoring missed: I counted margin dollars, not what the rule signals. Lesson for the criteria: a rule that only bites at the moments traders care about most is the most visible kind. The cut stays in the registry as a measured upper bound on what margin can do.

journal.title: Why giving the book more time does not work with an on-time mark
journal.body: At 20x, maintenance margin is 2.5% of notional and the takeover line is at 1.7%. P4 moves the mark up to 1% per update, so a position falling with the market crosses both in two or three updates, about 6–9 s, while HyperCore's partial liquidation wants 30 s between rounds. Lowering the takeover line or shortening the cooldown cannot create time that the margin does not have; it only takes over with less cushion. The old lagging mark gave the book time by accident, which is why GOOGL looked better under it. So the remaining lever is size: permanent tiers (T3: $2.67M, holds to 10 accounts, $21M of margin from the largest accounts) or the cluster rule (HL: $1.51M, split-proof). Open question for the user: is P4 alone acceptable, given every takeover already starts in profit on average, and the remaining risk is unwinding one whale's position?

journal.title: Per-account size rules are out
journal.body: Agreed with the user: tiers by dollar size or OI share only raise the number of wallets a whale needs. What remains split-proof is anything measured on the market as a whole rather than the account: the cluster rule (margin by how much size would be liquidated near the same price, needs Hyperliquid) or a global OI cap (deployer, but too coarse: the GOOGL whale was 8% of OI). So the margin side reduces to one question: is P4 alone acceptable, or is the cluster rule worth asking Hyperliquid for? If the latter, its own attacks (inflating a victim's cluster, laddering liquidation prices just over k apart) must be tested first.

journal.title: Margin settled: no margin change; the package is P4 alone
journal.body: The cluster rule is out too: an account's margin would depend on what other traders hold, which is unfair. With event cuts (signal) and per-account rules (split) already out, every margin lever we have is ruled out by robustness or fairness. Two lessons for my criteria: fairness means an account's requirements depend only on its own position, and 'traders don't feel it' includes what a rule signals, not just its cost. The package is P4 alone: deployer-only, robust to every bad-feed case tested, invisible in normal markets, takeovers in profit on average. What it leaves: the size the vault inherits (an unwind question, not a protocol one) and gaps faster than 1% per update (AMZN, about −$26k).

journal.title: Quiet days confirm it: traders would not notice P4
journal.body: Built six new coin-days (GOOGL, INTC, AMZN on Oct 20 and 21) through the same pipeline as the earnings days, about $2–4 of EC2 and pulls. Each validated at real parameters: relayer mark exact on every update, end-of-day positions 99.9–100% exact. P4 against today: mark a median 0.3–0.9 bp apart, as close or closer to the stock on five of six, smoother on all six; 35 accounts liquidated vs 36, none only under P4; 22 shares of stops fired only under P4 against about 2,000 only under today. One detail worth keeping: on Oct 21 overnight today's oracle trailed the feed by up to 21 bp, the clamp lagging an ordinary move; P4 removes that too. Quiet days are done; what remains for P4 is an illiquid coin and the round-2 price-discovery event.

journal.title: Illiquid coins are fine; discovery lives in closed-market pricing
journal.body: Instead of paying for an illiquid-coin extract, I rebuilt P4's trade price minute by minute for every xyz coin on the four days I have (469 coin-days). Its band would never have held: the widest gap between xyz trades and the feed was 9.5% on a 10% band. So thin coins behave like P2. The discovery screen surprised me. xyz does lead the feed, often, but almost entirely on Asian stocks and mostly while their home market is closed and the feed is frozen; trade.xyz already prices those hours internally. For US stocks out of hours with a live feed there is no lasting discovery episode on these days besides the earnings crashes. So the round-2 question is really about the internal regime, which is also where SKHX's $1M loss came from. That is a scope decision for the user.

journal.title: Out-of-hours is not closed-market
journal.body: The user pointed out that I was blurring two rules. They aren't the same: what decides is whether the feed is live, not the clock. US stocks out of hours are still an external session (oracle = E). Internal pricing is when E is frozen at the close and the oracle follows xyz's own book: weekends for US stocks, every weekday evening for Asian stocks (SKHX switches at 11:00 UTC). I re-labelled every minute by the relayer's own regime. P4 still never holds, but the closest call is now JIO on 10-28: its live feed jumped 9% at the Indian open, xyz refused to follow for 9 hours, and the gap peaked at 8.5% on a 10% band. That's the case to watch: if a live feed and xyz disagree by more than the band, P4 freezes the centre where today's formula would follow the feed. I can't yet say which side was right.

journal.title: JIO isn't discovery, it's a basis
journal.body: I expected JIO to be xyz leading or a bad feed. It's neither. The Indian session lifted the feed 14% (8% in under a minute), and xyz simply never followed. It stayed 3–6% below for two days, with negative funding not closing the gap. P4 and today's formula end up at the same place (median 4 bp apart, about 2.6% under E), because today's second mark input also converges to the book within 150 s. The two only differ in the first minutes after the jump, and only if the gap passes the band. Then P4 marks at xyz's price and today's formula marks at the band edge. For a coin nobody can arbitrage, the xyz price is where liquidations actually fill, so P4's choice looks right. But it also means a sustained xyz push beyond the band would freeze the centre: that's the g-p4-push test, now more urgent. The real damage on JIO came from today's internal → external hand-over the next morning (14 shorts forced out at marks above the book).

journal.title: Fake trades can freeze P4; adding the book fixes it
journal.body: I built the push attack I'd only argued about before. An attacker prints wash trades at a fixed price 6% above the GOOGL feed just before the crash. At $10M per 30 s nothing happens: the real crash volume outweighs them and the band follows the feed. At $50M per 30 s P4's band freezes, and the mark stays up to 4.4% above the market for as long as the attack lasts. In the replay that costs only fees, because the book never sees those prints. So P4 trusted one input, xyz trades, that an attacker can fake. The fix stays inside P4's own logic: the band may hold only if the xyz order book also disagrees with the feed (impact mid at Hyperliquid's 6,000 USDC funding notional). A bad feed print is contradicted by both trades and book, so P4b still blocks it, with identical results on all the bad-print and stuck-feed runs. Wash trades alone no longer move anything. To beat P4b an attacker has to hold the real book beyond the band, which means buying everything the crash sells at an above-market price. P4b is the new lead; it is still deployer-only.

journal.title: Holding the book is the expensive part
journal.body: I gave the attacker a bid 6% above the market, re-placed every block, buying everything offered below it. In the replay it can't win: makers keep re-quoting near the feed, it buys $112–132M of stock in a minute, and its bid is never standing when the relayer reads the book, so P4b never holds. That is partly an artefact of open-loop makers, so I priced it from the real tape instead. Just the real sellers in the crash would have cost it at least $2.8M in the first minute. The honest caveat is what happens if someone does pay. With the book and trades both at the attacker's price, P4b's mark can go to the old centre + 5% (+13% over the crashed feed), where today's formula would stop at the feed + 5%. P4b's hold has no time limit, and that is the remaining design choice: a limit as long as the longest bad print we want to block would cap this exposure.

journal.title: A hold that steps, not one that expires
journal.body: The obvious fix, letting the hold expire after 150 s, gives the problem back. A −20% feed print lasting five minutes walks the GOOGL mark down 16% and sends $8.1M of healthy positions to the vault, exactly like today. So the band shouldn't jump to the feed; it should walk toward it. Every 150 s (trade.xyz's own mark time constant, not a new number) the centre moves by at most its own width. The five-minute −20% print now moves the mark 32 bp. An attacker who props the book gets an edge over today that shrinks to zero within about two steps on the GOOGL crash. Everything else is identical to P4b. P4d is the new lead. It's still one sentence and deployer-only.

journal.title: Inherited notional is a whale problem
journal.body: Before choosing a margin lever I looked at who the vault actually inherits. On GOOGL it is essentially one isolated position: $12.2M at 16x, 91% of the inheritance. On INTC it is one $3.1M position at only 5.6x; INTC's gap is simply bigger than its margin. AMZN is the only spread-out case: hundreds of small accounts already past their initial margin. So the lever has to reduce notional held at high leverage into a gap, or the size of a single position against the book. The fair options left are a daily out-of-hours leverage schedule (the same for everyone, every day, not just earnings), a lower static max leverage per asset, or faster book liquidation of large positions (a Hyperliquid change).

journal.title: Earlier liquidation helps less once the mark is fast
journal.body: The user's point was that positions liquidated earlier would cost the vault less. The old test agreed: a ¾ buffer cut inherited 38% under today's slow mark. On P4d it only cuts 10–12%. P4d puts the gap into the mark within a couple of updates, so a position goes from healthy to takeover in 12–15 s and gets one 20% book clip before the vault takes the rest. A trigger at −1.25% instead of −2.5% is still inside an 8% gap. The speed-triggered buffer keeps most of the gain (−10%) and costs traders far less on quiet days: 50 extra liquidations over 6 coin-days, against 315 for a fixed ¾. It needs a Hyperliquid change (a variable MM ratio and a decoupled takeover level). To get a position liquidated before the gap, its liquidation price has to sit outside the gap. That is leverage again, not the trigger.

journal.title: The book is the ceiling
journal.body: Digging into why earlier liquidation helps so little on P4d: the book simply isn't big enough. Before GOOGL's onset, positions worth $17.3M had liquidation prices inside the coming 9.6% fall, against $7.6M of bids within 5% of the price. INTC and AMZN look the same ($7.8M vs $3.4M; $2.4M vs $2.5M). When the GOOGL whale's first 20% clip arrives, the top of the book holds about 900 shares against 7,500. Liquidation rules only decide who gets the book first; the rest goes to the vault either way. Valued at the feed 30 minutes later, the vault's inherited positions improve by 9–11% with the better buffers, no more. The lever that changes the total is how much notional has its liquidation price inside a plausible move, and that is set by leverage.

journal.title: Sell the excess, not a fixed slice
journal.body: Holding leverage was dropped: it forbids drawdowns. Liquidation timing only acts between MM and the takeover level, so I changed what a liquidation sells. Today a large position sells 20%, waits 30 s, and in a gap the vault takes the rest. Instead, sell just enough to put the account back at initial margin. On P4d across the three crashes the vault inherits $10.98M instead of $12.76M (−14%), as much as liquidating everything at once, while the trader keeps about half the position. Quiet days are unchanged. Restoring only to the MM line is worse ($16.07M): small positions that close in full today get trimmed and then gap into the takeover. With the speed-triggered buffer on top it reaches $9.90M, at the cost of 50 extra liquidations on quiet days. It needs a HyperCore change (liquidation order size) and adds no new constant.

journal.title: The vault's sales were never the problem
journal.body: Splitting the real vault's October losses against the external price: GOOGL lost $48k at takeover and $135k as the price kept falling while the vault held; its sales filled slightly above the external price. INTC and AMZN look the same. So the unwind loses by being slow, not by selling badly. Selling faster with bigger clips sells below fair value. Instead the vault can also take every bid at or above the oracle price: in a gap the xyz book lags the feed, so those stale bids are plentiful ($4.8M on GOOGL). On the replayed book this cuts the vault's exposure by 78 to 92% and its drift risk by about half to three quarters, and never sells below fair value. AMZN reminds us the realized drift is luck (it rebounded); the case rests on expectation, not on these paths.

journal.title: SKHX was a hand-over print
journal.body: The largest vault loss, SKHX on 07-27, was not a closed-market problem but a hand-over one. At 08:00 in Korea the external feed came back 22% below where it froze, while xyz was trading near its own price. The relayer jumped the oracle straight to the band edge (no clamp at the hand-over), the mark fell 1% per update, and the liquidations it started crushed the book; the vault inherited $27M of longs and was itself liquidated at the bottom. Two minutes later the feed printed 38% higher. Carrying P4d's band across the hand-over (the band starts from the internal price, the feed takes over only when it agrees with xyz's trades and book) keeps the mark at xyz's price throughout: none of the 945 positions held before the hand-over is liquidated. On 640 normal hand-overs the rule never fires. One rule now covers the external session and its hand-over.

journal.title: The three layers compose
journal.body: Run together on the three crashes and the two quiet days, the mark, liquidation and vault rules do not interfere: the fair sweep leaves every takeover exactly where restore-to-IM put it. Against today the vault inherits a little more ($10.98M vs $9.83M), because P4d lets the mark follow a real gap, but it inherits it at a positive value against the external price (+$57k instead of −$152k) with 300 underwater takeovers instead of 810, and then holds it a tenth as long (exposure −91%). Quiet days are identical on every layer. The package is ready to write up.

journal.title: The liquidation fee was half of HL's
journal.body: Every sim round that ran to its full size already matched HL; the excess was all in rounds the equity stop cut short. HL charges a liquidated account its own taker rate (0.864 or 0.9 bp), but prep averaged the fee over both sides of each liquidation fill, makers included, and got 0.43-0.56 bp. With each account's own rate, accounts matching HL's total liquidated size rise from 83/71/39% to 89/82/55%. A smaller per-account equity offset remains, most likely in the opening margin of isolated positions. Scenario tables need a rerun under the corrected fee.

journal.title: HyperCore's 1% cap binds
journal.body: Hyperliquid's own liquidation fills show a mark of 233.115 where the relayer published 233.0: HyperCore caps the final mark at 1% from the previous one (235.47 x 0.99). The sim had assumed the cap never binds and, where it was modelled, applied it to the relayer's inputs. Applied to the final mark, the sim's mark now equals Hyperliquid's at every liquidation block on all three crashes. What remains of the liquidation mismatch is a handful of cross-dex accounts and one market maker, not the liquidation rules.

journal.title: The parity fixes leave the design comparison unchanged
journal.body: The package and vault-unwind runs were redone with the per-user liquidation fee and HyperCore's 1% cap on the final mark. Every headline number moved by less than 0.1% (underwater takeovers under today 810 to 812) and the quiet days are identical. The fixes sharpen account-level parity; they do not change what the package does for the protocol.

journal.title: Cross accounts: one account, one liquidation
journal.body: Two bugs and one rule. Other-position margin was clamped event by event on unordered events, inventing up to $300 of margin requirement; it is now summed per block. And Hyperliquid liquidates a cross account on all its coins at once, in asset order: an account's INTC fills used its equity before its AMZN round, which stopped after 0.006 shares. The sim now reproduces that exactly. AMZN's excess liquidation falls from $15k to $2k, and its takeovers match Hyperliquid's to within 5% on every account.

journal.title: The benefits ledger
journal.body: Every test now has the package run against today on the same replay, and sim/benefits.py turns them into one ledger (docs/benefits.md). The package takes over more notional but at a profit against fair value (+0.52% vs −1.54%), holds a tenth of the exposure, and never dumps below fair value. Under every attack in the suite it ends better than today, and a −20% bad print that moves today's mark 18% moves it 34 bp. Its weak spot is the one P4d chose: it trusts xyz's own book within the band, so a buy wall can lift the mark up to 6% for a minute, at a cost to the attacker of $26–30M, 270 to 370 times what the vault loses (the smallest wall costs $7.5M and leaves the vault ahead).

journal.title: Capping the hold: rejected
journal.body: The ledger's weakest row was the buy wall: under P4d a wall at +6% lifts the mark up to 6.2% for a minute. A cap that stops a hold from moving the mark further from the feed than where it stood fixes that (6.2% to 1.2%), but it is the same move a stuck feed needs: when trade.xyz's feed freezes while xyz crashes, the hold must follow xyz away from it. The only signal that separates the two, whether the feed is moving, is too noisy over one update and too slow over 150 s. Every version that kept the wall out let a bad print or a stuck feed back in, so the package keeps P4d as it is; the wall costs its author 270 to 370 times what it costs the vault.

journal.title: The wall, made honest
journal.body: The buy-wall attacker was a phantom: no capital, no margin check, never liquidated, and post-only asks that would have crossed its bid filled against it instead of being rejected. As an ordinary margined account it behaves very differently: with $1M it is liquidated and taken over within a minute, and the vault's loss nearly vanishes. What remains is harm to traders: with $5M or more it held the package's mark 6% up for a minute and liquidated 73 accounts that are not liquidated otherwise. A hold-start rule (a hold may only begin when the feed jumps by more than the band within 30 s, or stops) halves that to 33, with no change on any other test, and is now part of the package. The rest is the price of letting xyz's own book lead within the band.

journal.title: Keep the clamp where the attacks come from
journal.body: With every attacker made to obey the engine, the package's weakness was plain: by letting xyz's own trades lead the mark, it let a funded buyer hold the mark 4–7% up during a crash, and the vault then took over that buyer's losing account at −$1.16M. Today's formula resists because its 50 bp clamp keeps xyz's book on a short leash; the same clamp is what makes it lag real crashes and follow bad prints. The lead design keeps the clamp only on the side attackers can buy: the mark follows trade.xyz's external price at once, xyz's book can pull it at most 50 bp, and xyz's own price takes over only when the external price jumps by more than the band in one update or stops. It keeps the crash and bad-print gains, matches today on pushes, and leaves normal markets exactly as they are.

journal.title: How much the vault needs
journal.body: xyz has already had the failure the vault exists to prevent: at SKHX on 07-27 the vault held $1.0M, inherited $25.6M of longs, ran out and was auto-deleveraged. Measured from the vault's own fills, it needs about 0.6–1.2% of a crashing market's OI to stay above its own maintenance margin under today's rules; under package_v 0.02–0.84%, and nothing at SKHX because the cascade never starts. Against $2.0B of xyz OI, one market the size of SP500 or SKHX gapping already needs $2–3M under today's rules; the vault holds $1.84M. If several markets can gap together, the need scales with their OI, up to about $24M (today) or $17M (package_v) if every xyz market moved like the worst event.

journal.title: Out of sample: a flaw found and fixed
journal.body: Seven markets on three days never used in the design (CL, BRENTOIL 09-10; META, GOOGL, SILVER 10-22; GOLD, SPCX 10-30), run on a spot instance in Tokyo. Parity at real parameters holds: mark exact at 72–100% of liquidation blocks (CL 160/177, BRENTOIL 155/173 are the weakest). package_v failed on oil: CME closes 21:00–22:00 UTC daily, the external price stands still, and package_v read that as a frozen feed, handing the mark to xyz's book. A 4-minute wick on xyz (CL 101 → 106.5, Brent to 110) then liquidated 91 CL and 79 BRENTOIL shorts that real HL and today's rules left alone. The fix (package_k): a quiet feed inside the venue's published closures is not a failure. Across the seven markets package_k liquidates 1,839 accounts on the book vs 1,867 today, takes over 57 times vs 76, inherits $1.26M vs $1.46M; GOLD, META, SPCX and the two quiet markets are unchanged. Cost: BRENTOIL's vault capital need rises from $5k to $15k (0.004% → 0.013% of its OI).

journal.title: package_k holds in sample, and closes a hole today's rules have
journal.body: Every in-sample scenario rerun under package_v and package_k: three crashes, two quiet days, normal markets, stuck feed, spikes, wash and wall attacks, and the 16-attack faithful suite. Every takeover, liquidation round and vault fill is identical; the marks differ only inside the 5-minute US-stock closure at 00:00 UTC, where package_v had drifted up to 63 bp from the frozen price. Then the attack the out-of-sample tape revealed, made faithful: a margined account props GOOGL's book 6% above mid during that closure. Under today's rules the mark climbs to +499 bp and 14 accounts are liquidated or taken over that would not be otherwise; under package_v the same (+500 bp, 14); under package_k the mark does not move beyond its no-attack level and no one is hurt, at every size ($1M–$25M) and length (60–240 s). Today's mark lets the book's premium walk to the discovery bound while the outside market is shut; package_k anchors the book input to E within 50 bp. The benefits ledger now benchmarks package_k (docs/benefits.md; package_v kept as benefits_pkgv.md).

journal.title: The closed-hours wick on oil: today's rules lose 147 accounts
journal.body: The same faithful attack on CL during CME's 60-minute daily close (09-10, from 21:10 UTC, ten minutes into the close and half an hour before the natural wick), run on a spot instance in Tokyo. A margined account with $1M bids 6% above the book for 60 s to 15 min. Under today's rules the mark climbs to the 5% discovery bound (+499 bp over the frozen price) and 147 accounts are liquidated or taken over that would not be otherwise (8 if it stops after a minute); the attacker spends $0.45M of its $1M doing it. Under package_k the mark moves at most 50 bp (today's per-update clamp, now anchored to E) and 3 small accounts close to liquidation are hit in the first minute, at every size and length. package_v hits 2–4 in this attack (why its frozen trigger stayed off here is not yet checked); the out-of-sample day is where it failed. CL's oracle stands still for an hour every weekday, so this exposure is daily.

journal.title: The engine missed two of trade.xyz's relayer rules; oil now replicates
journal.body: CL and BRENTOIL replayed worse than every other market (mark exact at 160/177 and 155/173 liquidation blocks, 19 and 12 takeovers seen only in reality). The cause was in the relayer model, not the clearing. (1) trade.xyz clamps its first mark price around the previous on-chain mark, not around the oracle (its docs: the 50 bp per-update clamp applies to the oracle and the mark component). On stocks and metals the mark never strays 50 bp from E, so the old model looked exact; oil's book sits 50–120 bp under E all day, so the clamp binds. (2) In the CME daily close (CL, BRENTOIL, SILVER, 21:00–22:00 UTC) and on weekends (GOLD, SPCX), the oracle is trade.xyz's internal oracle, a 30-minute moving average of xyz's book (fitted tau 1800 s, its documented value), not a frozen price. With both in the engine, CL reproduces the mark at 177/177 liquidation blocks and every real takeover (34 matched, 0 real-only); BRENTOIL 172/173 and 2 real-only; the other markets unchanged or better; stock crash days keep their parity. Under the faithful model today's rules take over 106 times on the seven markets (76 before) and package_k 57. The closed-hours wick on CL also changes: package_k still hurts 3–10 accounts where today's rules hurt 147, but a $5M attacker pushing for 15 minutes now hurts 55 under package_k (mark +216 bp), because the internal oracle follows the pushed book and package_k takes the oracle as its first input. The earlier '3 at every size' came from the frozen-oracle engine and is withdrawn.

journal.title: package_b: the daily break holds the closing price
journal.body: The faithful engine showed that a sustained push during CME's daily close drags trade.xyz's internal oracle (a 30-minute average of xyz's book), and package_k follows it (CL: $5M for 15 min, 55 accounts hurt). package_b keeps the last external price as the oracle through the daily break, since the outside market reopens within the hour, and keeps the internal oracle for weekends. On CL the attack now hurts 3 accounts at every size and length ($1M-$5M, 60 s-15 min; mark at most +50 bp), against 147-148 under today's rules. On the four CME markets' natural days (CL, BRENTOIL 09-10, SILVER 10-22, GOLD 10-30) package_b matches package_k to the account, so the hold costs honest trading nothing on these days. Weekends stay exposed: on GOLD (Fri 22:00 UTC, internal oracle) package_k and package_b hold for 4 minutes (0 accounts) but a 15-minute push moves the mark +259 bp and hurts 17 accounts; today's rules hurt 13 within a minute and 26 at 4 minutes.

journal.title: Two decisions: one rule for all closures; vault unwind out of the core
journal.body: package_b is withdrawn: a daily break must be treated like any other closed market. The fair sweep (vault unwind) leaves the package and becomes appendix material; the core package is the mark plus restore-to-IM. Next: one closed-market oracle rule that resists book pushes, tested on daily breaks and weekends alike.

journal.title: One closed-market rule: a capped internal oracle
journal.body: Holding the last external price through every closure would stop xyz from discovering price over weekends, and on 510 real internal sessions (109 markets) the frozen price is the worst guess at reopen (mean gap 71 bp vs 48 bp for trade.xyz's internal oracle). The candidate for all closures alike: keep the internal oracle (30-min EMA of xyz's book) but cap its input at c from the current oracle, so a push moves it at most about c/2 in 15 minutes. At c = 1% (Hyperliquid's per-update mark cap) the reopen gap is unchanged on average (47.8 vs 47.7 bp) and only 2 sessions end more than 50 bp further off; the worst is SKHX 07-27, a genuine -9% move over 6 h (189 bp vs 111 bp). At c = 0.5% pushes are bounded tighter (25 bp) but SKHX ends 582 bp off. Not yet run in the engine.

journal.title: A walking external feed: the core package was exposed; two relayer rules close it
journal.body: Question from the user: does following the external price at once (X1 = O = E) open the mark to a manipulated external feed? Yes. A feed walked 10% away over 15 s to 5 min (GOOGL, AMZN, 18:30 ET) never jumps more than d in one update, so package_k's feed-failure test never fires: the core package follows the walk at Hyperliquid's 1% per update and hands the vault $1.1-4.7M of healthy positions on the fast walks (today's clamp: $0.3-3.3M). Two relayer rules fix it. (1) A hold may also start when xyz's trades and book both disagree with E by more than the maintenance-margin rate (2.5% at 20x): fast and medium walks go to $0. (2) A held centre steps toward E only while xyz has no trades: the 5-minute walk, which the 150 s steps let through ($1.37M), goes to $0, mark -197 bp. Upward walks behave the same (one residual: $46k at 30 s). Checks: normal markets identical to the core package (the trigger never fires); crashes slightly better (underwater 322 -> 308); bad prints $0 with the -20%/5 min mark move -11 bp (from -42); stuck feed unchanged. Caveat: the replayed book does not react, so makers quoting off E could follow a manipulation in reality and weaken the trigger.

journal.title: The divergence trigger is rejected: it reopens the attack on xyz's own book
journal.body: Testing the user's dust-trade question exposed a bigger problem. (1) Correction: the first 'step only while stale' rule never stepped in practice, because xyz's trade price reaches back without a time limit; it was rebuilt with explicit freshness by trade count and by volume. (2) The divergence trigger (hold when xyz's trades and book disagree with E by more than the MM rate) was then run against the faithful attacks it was never tested on. Wash: two margined accounts trading $5M per update at +6% at the GOOGL crash lift the mark +1,443 bp and hurt 72 accounts, against +50 bp and 0-1 under the core package; prop: +594 bp against +50. All three release modes fail the same way. So the trigger trades protection against a manipulated external feed for exposure to a manipulated xyz market, and xyz's book is the cheaper of the two to manipulate. Decision: the core package (mark anchored to E within 50 bp, restore-to-IM) is the lead again. Its walking-feed exposure is real (a 10% walk over 15-30 s: $4.2-4.7M of healthy positions taken over, vs $1.1-3.3M today) and belongs at the source: how trade.xyz builds E (venue aggregation, staleness and divergence checks). The dust test as run was invalid (package rules inactive at 06:00 UTC in these preps) and is moot.

journal.title: E's source is where a manipulated external price must be stopped
journal.body: Two findings. (1) From the tape (126 xyz markets, 4 days): E's real weakness is staleness in thin sessions, not errors. Overnight (Blue Ocean), E is unchanged on 76% of updates and its longest frozen stretch is over 30 min on 95 of 280 US coin-days (90th percentile 3 h; BIRD, EBAY, BX, ZM, DKNG up to 8-13 h). The long E-vs-xyz disagreements were E-stale cases where xyz was right (SOXL 10-21: E frozen 2 h at 104.77 while xyz traded down; E resumed at 102.89). (2) No mark rule stops a sustained manipulated E: following it (core package), following it slower (today; corroborated speed, which only halves 15-30 s walks), or handing the mark to xyz (rejected: xyz is cheaper to manipulate). So the defense belongs in how trade.xyz builds E: its age, staleness handling, venues and quotes.

journal.title: A frozen E is priced like a closed market
journal.body: The core package's frozen-feed hold handed the mark to xyz's book whenever E froze in open hours, which is daily overnight. A 10-minute freeze plus a faithful attacker: wash $5M per update +481 bp, 20 accounts (today +17 bp); bids +6% above mid +484 bp, 19 accounts (today +500 bp, 19). Two fixes tested. B (lead): once E is unchanged for 2 updates the relayer prices the market with the capped internal oracle (1%), the same rule as scheduled closures, and a frozen feed no longer starts a hold: stale-E prop +50 bp / 0 accounts, wash +17 bp / 0. Cost: a genuine crash exactly while the feed is frozen (stuck feed at each crash onset) is followed late: value at takeover -$424k (today -$383k, core package +$8k), $15.3M inherited (today $14.0M). C (deeper book check) closed the wash but not the prop attack. Crashes, quiet days, normal markets and bad prints are identical for all. B fits criterion 1 (attacks first) and the one-rule principle; its cost case shrinks if trade.xyz's E stops freezing during live markets (E-source recommendations).

journal.title: SKHX 07-27 in the engine: the core package needs no capital to avoid ADL
journal.body: The one real ADL event now replays in the engine (mark exact at 163/192 liquidation blocks; vault inherits $27.06M vs $27.0M real). Under today's rules the vault needs $1.43M to avoid ADL; it held $1.01M, so ADL, as in reality. Under the core package it needs $0, and $1.04M to stay above its own maintenance margin (today $2.64M), even though it takes over more positions (491 vs 358): its takeovers happen at prices that keep it solvent. The closed-market caps (0.5/1/2%) give the same $0. The first run had replayed the real relayer before 17:45 UTC, so the internal session (11:00-23:00) was not simulated; fixed with a 12 h relayer warm-up.

journal.title: Closed-market oracle cap: 1%
journal.body: Engine runs of the capped internal oracle in every closure (CME daily break, weekends, the Korean night). Any cap closes the closed-market attack: CL daily close worst case 3 accounts / +50 bp (today 148 / +499, core package 55 / +216); GOLD weekend 0 accounts / +50-76 bp (today 26 / +400, core 17 / +259). Natural days on the 7 out-of-sample markets are unchanged and SKHX needs $0 to avoid ADL under every cap. The size is set by the screen of 510 real closures: 1% (Hyperliquid's per-update mark cap) tracks genuine moves as well as today at reopen (mean gap 47.8 bp vs 47.7) where 0.5% lags SKHX's genuine -9% by 582 bp and 2% doubles the push bound. Chosen: 1%, the cap B uses.

journal.title: Recommendations for how trade.xyz builds E
journal.body: Written into the LaTeX document (section 7) and the registry: publish E's age; overnight E from quotes and more than one venue; hold unconfirmed moves against E's own sources; alert on long E-vs-xyz disagreement without switching the mark. Each also shrinks the lead's one cost, a crash exactly while the feed is frozen.

journal.title: Study: what restore-to-IM does to xyz's book
journal.body: Per-round liquidation log (LIQ_ROUNDS_OUT) on the three crashes and the quiet days, 2 x 2: mark {today, lead} x sizing {20% every 30 s, restore-to-IM}; 22 positions start above $100k in each crash design, 1 on the quiet days (identical everywhere). Restore makes typical rounds larger (median $81k vs $47k, 6% vs 4% of the depth within 1%) but removes the dump rounds: today's sizing closes the rest in full during the 30 s cooldown, eating 116% of the 1% depth at the 90th percentile and moving the best price 105 bp (restore: 36%, 39 bp). Outcome: with the lead mark, restore moves $1.7M from the vault to the book (vault $10.66M -> $8.82M); with today's lagging mark it is slightly worse ($7.81M -> $8.49M), because it sizes from equity at a mark that overstates it in a crash. So restore-to-IM belongs with the mark fix, not alone. Cost: fills about 30 bp further below E; same-side liquidation rounds within 60 s +13% (crude). Limits: non-reacting book (impact is a lower bound); three crash days.

journal.title: Restore-to-IM on oil and metals: neutral on deep books
journal.body: The liquidation-size study on CL, BRENTOIL (09-10), SILVER (10-22) and GOLD (10-30): 19-22 positions start above $100k ($9.5-10.4M). Books were deep relative to them: 3-4% of the depth within 1% at the 90th percentile and about 1.5 bp per round (4 bp at the 90th percentile) under every rule. Restore needs fewer rounds (54 vs 66 with the lead mark) and same-side rounds within 60 s fall (226 vs 347); the vault takes little either way ($0.6-0.75M). So restore-to-IM's book cost is concentrated in thin, fast markets like the stock crashes, which is also where it moves the most from the vault to the book (with the lead mark).

journal.title: ADL comes from isolated-only markets; joint moves have not stressed the vault
journal.body: The whole xyz tape (392 days): $85.2M of ADL, all but SKHX 07-27 from markets while they were isolated-only (BRENTOIL $33M on 03-23, CL $9.9M, EWZ $9.3M, ...). Every market's ADL stopped once cross margin let the vault backstop it. On 11-05, the broadest selloff on record, all 25 backstop events were ADL on noCross markets and the vault took nothing. In the engine, the four real noCross ADL days give $196k today, $141k under the lead, $0 with cross enabled. A gap model on today's positions puts the vault's need for the worst real joint hour at $0.93M and four hours at $3.0M ($5.6M with cross everywhere), against $1.84M held; 'every market at its worst at once' ($6.9M for four hours) never happened.

journal.title: Vault capital from all positions: about a 10% yearly chance of exceeding $1.84M
journal.body: Capital need is now a function of every xyz position: today's 100,512 positions under every real hour of 120 markets, with an extreme-value tail for probabilities. The vault's $1.84M is exceeded in about 10% of years (90% interval 0-49%), the 1-in-10-year need is $1.85M and the 1-in-100-year $3.3M (0.96-18). A uniform 5% gap across xyz needs $2.6M, 10% needs $10.6M. Backtest roughly calibrated, slightly under-predicting the tail. The rule can be recomputed every morning from the snapshot.

journal.title: The proposal written up
journal.body: docs/mark_formulas.tex now opens with the proposal: seven changes (relayer: oracle follows E with the book clamped to E, feed-failure holds, one rule whenever E is not live; Hyperliquid: restore-to-IM; trade.xyz: cross margin on isolated-only markets, with a Hyperliquid fallback, a daily capital rule from all positions, a better E), the mark in one formula, the table of what changes, the first markets to move to cross, the capital figures, and the costs and limits. The variants follow as evidence.

journal.title: Cross margin only where Hyperliquid allows it: six markets
journal.body: Hyperliquid's HIP-3 rules gate cross margin (irreversible; validators require liquidity, a reliable oracle and manipulation resilience; a 50% daily move triggers a slashing review), and trade.xyz's backstop liquidator only serves cross-enabled assets. Scored against the weakest of the 22 markets already cross-enabled, 6 of the 98 isolated-only markets qualify: HOOD, MSTR, NBIS, AMD, EWY, SAMSUNG ($167M OI). They cut the worst real hour's isolated-only ADL from $10.0M to $6.8M and add $0.6M to the 4-hour capital need. The proposal now asks for cross margin on these six only; the markets with past isolated-only ADL (EWZ, UNITREE, NOW, LITE, MRVL, RDDT, ...) are not eligible and remain the residual.
